It motivates the geometric product from what the inner and cross products cannot do, compresses the answer into the one rule $v^{2} = Q(v)$, introduces blades and grades, explains what a signature is and why mixed signatures contain null vectors, presents the two canonical involutions, constructs rotors and the groups $\Pin$ and $\Spin$, and states the mod-8 classification of the real Clifford algebras. It then describes the conformal model, in which the oldest division by zero, $1/0$, is resolved by a projective completion. It closes with a toolkit that proves the classical structural lemmas the series imports: the commutation rule, the twisted adjoint action, the centre and pseudoscalar computations behind the classification (whose induction is cited, not repeated), and the splitting lemma. Every idea is introduced through a worked example, verified by machine in exact arithmetic. Each section names where the series uses its content, so the primer also serves as a reading route. The primer does not treat the failure of division: zero divisors, pseudo-inverses, and the taxonomy of obstructions are assigned entirely to T1, definitions and proofs alike. This is an expository companion, not a research contribution: nothing in it is new, and it carries no epistemic tier. t00-regenerated.title: What this primer is, and is not
t00-regenerated.text:
The Transport Papers are a series about what happens where division fails in a Clifford algebra. The series' research papers hold themselves to a strict standard: complete proofs, declared hypotheses, machine verification. That standard leaves no room for slow explanations, and a reader meeting geometric algebra for the first time deserves slow explanations. This primer supplies them.

The plan is short. the section ``Products of vectors, and the one rule'' asks what a product of vectors ought to do, shows that the two products of ordinary vector algebra do not do it, and arrives at the geometric product and the single rule that generates it. the section ``Blades and grades'' shows what the resulting algebra looks like inside. the section ``Signature, and the arrival of null vectors'' explains signature, and why mixed signatures contain the null vectors that are the series' central subject. the section ``The two involutions'' introduces the two canonical involutions. the section ``Rotors: how the algebra moves things'' builds rotors, reflections, and the groups $\Pin$ and $\Spin$. the section ``The mod-8 classification'' states the mod-8 classification. the section ``The conformal model, and the oldest division by zero'' describes the conformal model and the oldest resolved division by zero. the section ``The toolkit: the classical lemmas the series imports'' collects, with complete proofs, the classical structural lemmas that T1 \cite{ButlerT1} imports. the section ``Notation at a glance'' is a one-page table of the symbols the series uses, for a reader who meets one before its section. the section ``A reading route'' is a reading route through the series. What happens where division fails, the question the series exists to answer, is deliberately not treated here: it is assigned to T1, and the section ``Signature, and the arrival of null vectors'' stops where that question begins. A reader who already works with the inner and outer products can begin at the section ``Blades and grades'' and use the section ``Products of vectors, and the one rule'' only to fix notation.

Three warnings, so that the primer is used correctly. First, it is bounded: no geometric calculus, no applications, no physics. The textbooks do all of that better \cite{Macdonald2010, DoranLasenby2003, DFM2007, HestenesSobczyk1984}. Second, the part used in the series' proofs is exactly one section: the research papers state every fact they use, and the toolkit of the section ``The toolkit: the classical lemmas the series imports'' is where the classical facts among them are proved (save the classification theorem, which the toolkit states with the classical sources cited for its induction). T1 restates the toolkit's lemmas, with their numbers here, and cites this primer for the proofs; everything before the toolkit is a convenience, so that a reader has an easy place to start. Third, it is not new: everything here is classical, and the classical sources are cited section by section \cite{Porteous1995, Lounesto2001, Lam2005, Chevalley1997, ABS1964}.

t00-regenerated.title: Products of vectors, and the one rule
t00-regenerated.text:
Adding vectors causes no trouble. Two displacements compose into a third, the picture and the algebra agree, and there is nothing to explain. What is wanted next is a product: a way of multiplying two vectors that is associative, that keeps the geometry of the pair, and that can be undone, so that knowing $a$ and the product $ab$ recovers $b$. Multiplication and division of vectors, on the same footing as multiplication and division of numbers. That is the whole demand, and it is worth being precise about how the products a reader already knows fall short of it, because the geometric product is built to repair exactly those faults.

Ordinary vector algebra in three dimensions offers two products. The inner product $a \cdot b = |a|\,|b| \cos\theta$ returns a number. It knows lengths and angles, which is most of Euclidean geometry, but it is symmetric in its two arguments and retains nothing about the plane they span. The cross product $a \times b$ returns a vector perpendicular to both, of length $|a|\,|b| \sin\theta$. It does record that plane, but it records it by pointing away from it, and that device is available in three dimensions only: in a plane there is no perpendicular direction to point along, and in four dimensions there are too many, since the vectors orthogonal to a given pair form a plane rather than a line.

Both products have a second limitation, and for this series it is the decisive one. Neither can be undone. Knowing $a$ and the number $a \cdot b$ does not determine $b$, and knowing $a$ and the vector $a \times b$ does not either. There is no division, and no candidate for one. A subject whose question is what happens where division fails cannot start there.

t00-regenerated.title: Products of vectors, and the one rule
t00-regenerated.text: \textbf{What each product throws away, the other keeps.} The inner product keeps the cosine and discards the plane; the cross product keeps the plane and the sine. Each fails to be invertible exactly where it returns zero, and they return zero in complementary places: $a \cdot b$ vanishes when $b$ is perpendicular to $a$, $a \times b$ when $b$ is parallel to it, and for $a \neq 0$ both vanish only when $b = 0$. Between them they hold everything about the pair. So a single product that carried both pieces at once, the number and the plane, would have lost nothing, and would have a chance of being invertible. That is the product to build, and two questions stand in the way. What should record the plane of $a$ and $b$ in dimensions above three, where no perpendicular vector is available to stand in for it? And what does it mean to add a plane element to a number?

t00-regenerated.title: Products of vectors, and the one rule
t00-regenerated.text:
\textbf{The outer product answers the first.} Grassmann's answer, published in 1844, was to let the plane element be the object itself rather than a perpendicular substitute for it. The \emph{outer product} $a \wedge b$ is the oriented parallelogram spanned by $a$ and $b$: a plane, an area $|a|\,|b| \sin\theta$, and a sense of circulation around it. Exchanging the factors reverses that sense, so the product is antisymmetric,
\[
a \wedge b \;=\; -\, b \wedge a , \qquad \text{and in particular} \qquad a \wedge a \;=\; 0 .
\]
Only the plane, the area and the sense are recorded, not the particular parallelogram: $a \wedge (b + \lambda a) = a \wedge b$ for every scalar $\lambda$, so sliding one edge along the other changes nothing. Because the definition never mentions a perpendicular direction, it makes sense in every dimension. The object it produces is a \emph{bivector}, and it is not a vector. In three dimensions a bivector carries the same information as $a \times b$, which is why the cross product serves so well there, and why it does not generalise.

The construction does not stop at two vectors. The outer product is associative, so three vectors give $a \wedge b \wedge c$, the oriented parallelepiped they span: a three-dimensional subspace, the volume of that parallelepiped, and a handedness. That object is a \emph{trivector}. Four vectors give an oriented four-dimensional volume, and so on, the outer product of $k$ independent vectors representing the oriented $k$-dimensional subspace they span, weighted by its $k$-dimensional content. The antisymmetry that gave $a \wedge a = 0$ makes the outer product of any linearly dependent set vanish, so in an $n$-dimensional space the sequence ends at $k = n$: scalars, vectors, bivectors, trivectors, and upward to a single top object with nothing above it. That ceiling is not a convention. It is the statement that any $n+1$ vectors of an $n$-dimensional space are dependent.

t00-regenerated.title: Products of vectors, and the one rule
t00-regenerated.text:
\textbf{Clifford's step answers the second.} Keep both parts, and add them:
\[
ab \;=\; a \cdot b \;+\; a \wedge b .
\]
The objection is immediate: a number and a plane element are different kinds of object, and adding them looks like a mistake. The sum claims nothing about numbers and areas being the same kind of thing. It is bookkeeping: the two parts are kept in one symbol because they travel together and the pair is more useful than the pieces, in the way a real part and an imaginary part are kept together in one complex number. Elements that combine objects of several kinds in this way are called \emph{multivectors}.

What the sum buys is division. Take $b = a$: the outer part vanishes, and the product of a vector with itself is the pure number $a \cdot a$, its squared length. So whenever that number is not zero the vector has a two-sided inverse,
\[
a^{-1} \;=\; \frac{a}{a \cdot a} ,
\]
which is what neither the inner nor the outer product could supply alone. Clifford, in 1878, joined Grassmann's outer product to Hamilton's quaternions in exactly this way, and the algebra that results is the subject of this primer.

t00-regenerated.title: Products of vectors, and the one rule
t00-regenerated.text:
\textbf{One rule generates all of it.} That last observation is also the definition. If the square of every vector is a number, then polarising recovers both products, so nothing is lost by taking the one statement as the axiom and deriving the rest.

Start with a real vector space $\mathbb{V}$ carrying a quadratic form $Q$, which assigns to each vector $v$ a number $Q(v)$, its squared length. The \emph{geometric product} is the associative product generated by the vectors of $\mathbb{V}$ subject to one rule:
\[
v^{2} \;=\; Q(v) \qquad \text{for every vector } v .
\]
A vector times itself is a scalar. Everything else follows from this rule and associativity, and the algebra it generates is the \emph{Clifford algebra} $\Cl(\mathbb{V}, Q)$, called the \emph{geometric algebra} of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ when one wants to emphasise the geometry.

The two products return at once. Replace $v$ by $a + b$ in the rule and expand:
\[
(a+b)^{2} = a^{2} + ab + ba + b^{2}, \qquad \text{so} \qquad ab + ba \;=\; 2\, a \cdot b ,
\]
where $a \cdot b = \tfrac12\bigl(Q(a+b) - Q(a) - Q(b)\bigr)$ is the inner product obtained by polarising $Q$. So the symmetric part of the geometric product is the inner product, and \emph{orthogonal vectors anticommute}: if $a \cdot b = 0$ then $ab = -ba$. The antisymmetric part is the outer product of a figure of the original,
\[
a \wedge b \;=\; \tfrac12 (ab - ba), \qquad \text{so that} \qquad ab \;=\; a \cdot b \;+\; a \wedge b ,
\]
which is the decomposition this section arrived at geometrically. The rule constrains only the symmetric half, so the antisymmetric half is new content rather than something the axiom fixes; and that this half is the outer product already defined, and not merely some antisymmetric quantity, is what Example \claimref{note.primer.euclidean-plane} checks, where it comes out as the signed area of the parallelogram times the unit bivector. The product of two vectors is a scalar plus a bivector, and the bivector represents the oriented plane the two vectors span, weighted by the area of their parallelogram.

t00-regenerated.title: The Euclidean plane
t00-regenerated.text:
Let $e_1, e_2$ be an orthonormal basis of the Euclidean plane: $e_1^{2} = e_2^{2} = 1$ and $e_1 \cdot e_2 = 0$, so $e_1 e_2 = -e_2 e_1$. Multiply two general vectors $a = a_1 e_1 + a_2 e_2$ and $b = b_1 e_1 + b_2 e_2$:
\[
ab \;=\; (a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2) \;+\; (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)\, e_1 e_2 .
\]
The scalar part is the dot product; the coefficient of $e_1 e_2$ is the signed area. One product carries both. Now square the bivector:
\[
(e_1 e_2)^{2} \;=\; e_1 e_2 e_1 e_2 \;=\; - e_1 e_1 e_2 e_2 \;=\; -1 .
\]
The unit bivector of the Euclidean plane squares to $-1$. The even elements $\alpha + \beta\, e_1 e_2$ therefore multiply exactly like complex numbers: the complex plane is contained in the geometric algebra of the real plane, as its even half, and the imaginary unit is the plane's own unit of oriented area. The invertible product the plane has had since the eighteenth century, complex multiplication, is therefore not an ingredient of the construction but a consequence of it.

t00-regenerated.title: Blades and grades
t00-regenerated.text:
Fix an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of $\mathbb{V}$. Because orthogonal vectors anticommute and each $e_i^{2}$ is a scalar, any product of basis vectors can be reordered and reduced until each index appears at most once. The surviving products
\[
1, \quad e_i, \quad e_i e_j \ (i<j), \quad e_i e_j e_k \ (i<j<k), \quad \dots, \quad e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n
\]
are the \emph{basis blades}, and they form a linear basis of the algebra: one blade for each subset of the indices, hence
\[
\dim \Cl(\mathbb{V}, Q) \;=\; 2^{n} .
\]
This count holds even when $Q$ is degenerate \cite{Chevalley1997}, a fact the series needs exactly once, in an essential step of one of T1's proofs.

A blade built from $k$ distinct vectors has \emph{grade} $k$, and the grades are exactly the objects the section ``Products of vectors, and the one rule'' built: scalars are grade 0, vectors grade 1, the bivectors grade 2, the trivectors grade 3, and so on up to the single top blade $\omega = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n$, the \emph{pseudoscalar}, which represents the oriented volume of the whole space and is the top element that section's dependence argument located. Grade is basis-independent \cite{Porteous1995}, so the algebra splits into graded pieces, one for each dimension of geometric object it can represent: points of measure, directions, planes, volumes, and so on up to the space itself. The geometric product moves between the grades; the inner and outer products of the section ``Products of vectors, and the one rule'' are its grade-lowering and grade-raising parts.

t00-regenerated.title: Signature, and the arrival of null vectors
t00-regenerated.text:
Over the reals, a nondegenerate quadratic form can be brought to a diagonal shape in which $p$ basis vectors square to $+1$ and $q$ square to $-1$; the pair $(p,q)$ is the \emph{signature}, and it is an invariant (Sylvester's law \cite{Lam2005}). Write $\Cl(p,q)$ for the corresponding algebra. Euclidean space is $(n, 0)$; the spacetime of physics is $(1,3)$: one time direction of positive square, three space directions of negative square.

Signatures with $p, q \geq 1$ are called \emph{mixed}, and something qualitatively new happens there. Positive and negative squares can cancel:
\[
v \;=\; e_1 + e_n, \qquad v^{2} \;=\; e_1^{2} + e_n^{2} \;=\; 1 - 1 \;=\; 0 \qquad (e_1^2 = 1,\ e_n^2 = -1).
\]
(The cross terms $e_1 e_n + e_n e_1 = 2\,e_1 \cdot e_n$ vanish because the basis is orthogonal.) A nonzero vector whose square is zero is called \emph{null} (or isotropic). Null vectors fill a cone, the \emph{null cone}, and in spacetime that cone is the light cone: the null directions are the paths light takes. In a definite signature there are no null vectors at all; $Q(v) = 0$ forces $v = 0$.

A vector with $Q(v) \neq 0$ has the inverse $v^{-1} = v / Q(v)$, since $v\,(v/Q(v)) = v^2/Q(v) = 1$; a null vector has none, and what that failure means, and what can be done about it, is the series' opening question. This primer stops here: the failure of division, its taxonomy, and its repair are assigned to T1, from the first definition onward.
t00-regenerated.label: note

t00-regenerated.title: The hyperbolic plane
t00-regenerated.text:
The smallest mixed signature is $(1,1)$, the \emph{hyperbolic plane}, and it is the smallest unit from which the whole subject is built. Set
\[
v \;=\; \tfrac12 (e_1 + e_2), \qquad w \;=\; \tfrac12 (e_1 - e_2) \qquad (e_1^2 = 1,\ e_2^2 = -1).
\]
Then $v^{2} = w^{2} = 0$: both are null. But their cross terms survive:
\[
vw + wv \;=\; 2\, v\cdot w \;=\; 2\cdot\tfrac14\,(e_1 + e_2)\cdot(e_1 - e_2) \;=\; \tfrac12\bigl(Q(e_1) - Q(e_2)\bigr) \;=\; 1 .
\]
A pair of null vectors with $vw + wv = 1$ is a \emph{hyperbolic pair}, and it satisfies the identity
\[
v\,w\,v \;=\; (1 - wv)\,v \;=\; v - w v^2 \;=\; v .
\]
Multiplying by $v$, then $w$, then $v$ returns $v$ exactly. What this identity means for the failure of division is the opening theme of T1; here it is simply an exact computation worth checking by hand.

t00-regenerated.title: The two involutions
t00-regenerated.text:
Two canonical symmetries act on every Clifford algebra, both fixed by what they do to vectors.

The \emph{grade involution} $x \mapsto \hat{x}$ sends every vector to its negative, $\hat{v} = -v$, and extends multiplicatively: $\widehat{xy} = \hat{x}\hat{y}$. On a blade of grade $k$ it gives the sign $(-1)^{k}$, so it fixes the even grades and negates the odd ones. It is the algebraic counterpart of the point reflection $x \mapsto -x$.

The \emph{reversion} $x \mapsto \tilde{x}$ fixes every vector, $\tilde{v} = v$, but reverses the order of products: $\widetilde{xy} = \tilde{y}\tilde{x}$. On a blade of grade $k$ it gives the sign $(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$, the sign produced by reversing $k$ anticommuting factors. It plays the role that transposition plays for matrices and conjugation plays for complex numbers.

One consequence is used constantly. If a vector $v$ is orthogonal to every vector appearing in an element $x$, then moving $v$ past $x$ produces exactly a grade involution:
\[
v\,x \;=\; \hat{x}\,v .
\]
For a single orthogonal vector this is just anticommutation; the general case follows because both sides are multiplicative in $x$.

t00-regenerated.title: Rotors: how the algebra moves things
t00-regenerated.text:
Geometric algebra does not act on vectors through matrices; it acts through its own elements, by a sandwich product. The basic case is the reflection. For an invertible vector $u$, the map
\[
x \;\longmapsto\; -\,u\,x\,u^{-1}
\]
is the reflection of the vector $x$ in the hyperplane orthogonal to $u$: it fixes everything orthogonal to $u$ (which anticommutes past $u$, absorbing the minus sign) and negates $u$ itself. Every isometry of a nondegenerate quadratic space is a product of reflections (the Cartan--Dieudonn\'e theorem \cite{Lam2005}), so products of invertible vectors, called \emph{versors}, reach every element of the orthogonal group $O(p,q)$.

The group formed by versors whose factors are normalised to $Q(u) = \pm 1$ is called $\Pin(p,q)$; its even part, products of an even number of unit vectors, is $\Spin(p,q)$, and covers the rotations. An even versor $R$ with $R\tilde{R} = 1$ is a \emph{rotor}, and it acts by plain conjugation, $x \mapsto R\,x\,R^{-1}$, two reflections making one rotation. One more name the series uses: $\Spin^0(p,q)$ is the \emph{identity component} of $\Spin(p,q)$, the elements joined to $1$ by a continuous path inside the group; in a definite signature of dimension at least two it is all of $\Spin$, while in mixed signature it is a proper subgroup. The precise action of a general versor, including the odd ones, needs a small twist by the grade involution; it is set out and proved in the toolkit (Lemma \claimref{primer.twisted-adjoint-action}).
t00-regenerated.label: note

t00-regenerated.title: A rotation, exactly
t00-regenerated.text:
In the Euclidean plane of Example \claimref{note.primer.euclidean-plane}, take $R = a - b\,e_1 e_2$ with $a, b$ real, not both zero (a rotor once normalised by $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$; the conjugation below ignores the scale). Its reverse is $\tilde{R} = a + b\, e_1 e_2$ and $R\tilde{R} = a^{2} + b^{2}$, so $R^{-1} = \tilde{R}/(a^2 + b^2)$. Conjugating $e_1$:
\[
R\, e_1\, R^{-1} \;=\; \frac{a^{2} - b^{2}}{a^{2} + b^{2}}\, e_1 \;+\; \frac{2ab}{a^{2} + b^{2}}\, e_2 .
\]
The coefficients are the cosine and sine of the double angle of the point $(a,b)$: the rotor rotates $e_1$ towards $e_2$ by $2\arctan(b/a)$, and with $a, b$ rational every entry is exactly rational. (The sign in $R$ is the usual half-angle convention, $R = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2} - \sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\, e_1 e_2$; the sign is easy to get wrong, and the machine check below verifies it.) This is the half-angle representation of rotations, and it is why rotors, like quaternions, cover the rotation group twice: $R$ and $-R$ rotate identically.

t00-regenerated.title: A boost, and what it does to a null direction
t00-regenerated.text:
In the hyperbolic plane $\Cl(1,1)$, even elements $R = a + b\, e_1 e_2$ have $R\tilde R = a^2 - b^2$, so rotors satisfy $a^{2} - b^{2} = 1$: they are the \emph{boosts}, the hyperbolic rotations of special relativity. Conjugating the null vector $v = \tfrac12(e_1 + e_2)$ of Example \claimref{note.primer.hyperbolic-plane}:
\[
R\,v\,R^{-1} \;=\; (a - b)^{2}\, v \qquad \text{(exactly, using } (a-b)(a+b) = 1\text{)}.
\]
A boost does not move the null direction; it \emph{rescales} it. The null lines are the boost's eigendirections, with reciprocal eigenvalues $(a \mp b)^{2}$. This one computation underlies a great deal of physics: it is why horizons redshift, and in the series it is why the completed algebra at a black-hole singularity carries a preferred one-parameter flow.

t00-regenerated.title: The mod-8 classification

Every real Clifford algebra is a matrix algebra, or a pair of matrix algebras, over $\R$, $\C$ or $\HH$, and which one depends only on $p - q$ modulo 8 \cite{ABS1964, Porteous1995, Lounesto2001}:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cl@{\qquad}cl}
\toprule
$p-q \bmod 8$ & type & $p-q \bmod 8$ & type \\
\midrule
$0$ & $\Mat_k(\R)$              & $4$ & $\Mat_k(\HH)$ \\
$1$ & $\Mat_k(\R) \oplus \Mat_k(\R)$ & $5$ & $\Mat_k(\HH) \oplus \Mat_k(\HH)$ \\
$2$ & $\Mat_k(\R)$              & $6$ & $\Mat_k(\HH)$ \\
$3$ & $\Mat_k(\C)$              & $7$ & $\Mat_k(\C)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent In each case the matrix size $k$ is fixed by the dimension count $2^{n}$. The small algebras are worth knowing by name: $\Cl(1,0) \cong \R \oplus \R$ (residue 1, split), $\Cl(0,1) \cong \C$ (residue 7), $\Cl(2,0) \cong \Cl(1,1) \cong \Mat_2(\R)$ (residues 2 and 0), $\Cl(0,2) \cong \HH$ (residue 6), $\Cl(0,3) \cong \HH \oplus \HH$ (residue 5), and the spacetime algebra $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat_2(\HH)$ (residue 6). The doubled rows, residues 1 and 5, are the \emph{split} algebras, the ones that decompose into two ideals; what that means for division is T1's type-C case.

The table repeats with period 8, and the repetition has a mechanism: adding one $(+1)$ and one $(-1)$ direction at once leaves $p - q$ unchanged and doubles the matrix size,
\[
\Cl(p{+}1,\, q{+}1) \;\cong\; \Mat_2\bigl(\Cl(p,q)\bigr),
\]
the $(1,1)$-periodicity theorem. This matters here, because the added $(+1,-1)$ pair spans exactly a hyperbolic plane: the unit of Example \claimref{note.primer.hyperbolic-plane} is also the unit of the classification's own periodicity.

t00-regenerated.title: The conformal model, and the oldest division by zero
t00-regenerated.text:
The final construction is the one the series turns into a principle. Take a quadratic space $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ of signature $(p,q)$ and adjoin two extra directions $e_+, e_-$ with $e_+^{2} = +1$, $e_-^{2} = -1$: one hyperbolic plane, giving $\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$. Out of the new plane build the null pair
\[
n_0 = \tfrac12(e_- - e_+), \qquad n_\infty = e_- + e_+ ,
\]
representing the origin and the point at infinity, and represent each point $x \in \mathbb{V}$ by the vector
\[
X(x) \;=\; n_0 + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\, n_\infty .
\]
A short computation gives $X(x)^{2} = 0$: every point of the space is represented by a \emph{null} vector in the enlarged space, determined up to scale, so points become null rays on a quadric. The lift also remembers the geometry exactly, since $X(x) \cdot X(y) = -\tfrac12\,Q(x - y)$. This is the \emph{conformal model} of geometric algebra \cite{Hestenes2001, DFM2007, DoranLasenby2003}, and its power is that the conformal transformations of $\mathbb{V}$, inversions included, all become sandwich products in the enlarged algebra.

What this primer takes from the model is the oldest division by zero. Take the real line, $\mathbb{V} = \R$ with $Q(x) = x^{2}$. The reciprocal $x \mapsto 1/x$ fails at the origin. In the enlarged space, the quadric is a circle, the projective line $\R P^{1}$ in homogeneous coordinates $[\,x : s\,]$, and the reciprocal becomes the linear swap $[\,x : s\,] \mapsto [\,s : x\,]$, which is total: it never fails anywhere. At the origin it gives $[\,0 : 1\,] \mapsto [\,1 : 0\,]$, the point at infinity. Division by zero has an answer; the answer simply is not a real number, and it lies in the completion. Nothing here is new: this is the nineteenth-century projective resolution of $1/0$, the same construction that makes M\"obius maps $z \mapsto (az+b)/(cz+d)$ total on the Riemann sphere.

What the series adds, and this is the point at which the reader should turn to T1, is a uniqueness claim: for a general quadratic space this completion is not one convenient construction among many but the \emph{unique minimal} resolution of the null cone's division failure, the repair of the element itself being provably impossible. The construction becomes a theorem.

The series is eighteen papers, T0 to T17, in six arcs. This primer is T0. t01-regenerated.title: Introduction
t01-regenerated.text:
In ordinary arithmetic, division fails at exactly one number, and the failure is handled by prohibition: division by zero is forbidden, and every calculation routes around it. This paper is about the same failure in a richer setting. A Clifford algebra is the algebra of a geometry: its elements are built from the vectors of a space, and its one rule is that a vector times itself is its squared length. In such an algebra most elements can be divided by. Every vector of nonzero length has an exact inverse, and these invertible elements are plentiful enough to build every symmetry of the underlying space \cite{HestenesSobczyk1984, DoranLasenby2003}. But with three exceptions (the real numbers, the complex numbers and the quaternions, the three Clifford algebras that are themselves division algebras), every real Clifford algebra also contains nonzero elements that cannot be inverted at all: elements that multiply with some partner to give exactly zero, the \emph{zero divisors}. Where they occur, division fails, and the standard response is arithmetic's response: exclude them and work around the exclusion.

The response examined here is the opposite one, and it is the founding idea of the programme this paper begins: read each failure of division as an instruction. A failure, precisely located, tells you what the algebra is missing. The theorems of this paper show that it also tells you the smallest thing that can be added to supply it, and that the addition is forced, not chosen.

The stance has a precedent in the foundations of mathematics, and the precedent was in fact the founding idea's model. G\"odel proved that any consistent system strong enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. The famous part is the impossibility; the instructive part is its precision. The unprovable statement is informative: it names, exactly, the stronger system in which it becomes a theorem, and that stronger system contains new unprovable statements of its own, without end. This paper proves that division by zero in a Clifford algebra has the same structure. The impossibility is internal and exact: an inverse of a null vector $v$ would satisfy $vv^{-1} = 1$, and multiplying by $v$ reduces it to $v = 0$ (Lemma \claimref{transport.noinverse}). The failure determines its own repair, exactly one hyperbolic plane, which is the minimality half of the type-N theorems. And the completed algebra carries a new null cone of its own, so the ascent never terminates; the resulting tower is the subject of T3 \cite{ButlerT3}. The parallel is structural, not a theorem, since provability and invertibility belong to different categories, and nothing below depends on it. What it supplies is the right way to read what follows: the limit of a system indicates the system that removes it, and mathematics has met this kind of obstruction before.

The failures come in exactly three kinds, each with a concrete description. A \emph{null vector} is a direction whose squared length is zero; in spacetime these are the directions light travels, and no algebra containing such a vector can invert it. An \emph{idempotent} is an element with $e^2 = e$, one of the algebra's projections; every projection other than $0$ and $1$ annihilates its complementary projection, so each is a zero divisor. And in certain signatures the algebra splits into two independent halves that annihilate each other; the \emph{central} idempotents that effect this split are the deepest failure of the three, because no symmetry of the algebra can even exchange the halves. We prove this list complete: every zero divisor belongs to one of the three kinds. For each kind the paper then proves the repair. The null vector cannot be repaired as an element: once the space has more than two dimensions, no assignment of pseudo-inverses (the standard weakened substitute for an inverse, recalled in the section ``Setting, and the classical facts the proofs use'') can respect the symmetries of the space, whether valued in the algebra itself, in the Clifford algebra of any extension of the space, or in a matrix algebra over one (the scope of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} and Remark \claimref{note.transport.obstruction-parabolic}); the two-dimensional hyperbolic plane is the only exception, and an instructive one. What can be repaired is the space of points itself, by a completion that costs exactly one new plane and makes the reciprocal total; no smaller completion works. The split algebra is repaired by one added generator, which fuses its two halves into a single simple algebra, again minimally. The ordinary projection turns out to need no repair at all: it is its own pseudo-inverse. And the repairs compose cleanly, so a repair never creates a failure it cannot finish.

The plan of the paper is the plan just sketched, now with theorems attached. First classify: the three kinds have sharp existence loci, and the classification is exhaustive (the section ``A taxonomy of obstructions''). t01-regenerated.title: Quadratic spaces and Clifford algebras
t01-regenerated.text:
$(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is a finite-dimensional real quadratic space with polarisation $a \cdot b = \tfrac12(Q(a+b) - Q(a) - Q(b))$, so $a \cdot a = Q(a)$, and is \emph{nondegenerate} when $a \cdot b = 0$ for all $b$ forces $a = 0$. It then has an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ with $e_i^{\,2} \mathrel{:=} Q(e_i) = +1$ for $p$ vectors and $-1$ for the remaining $q = n-p$; the \emph{signature} $(p,q)$ is an invariant (Sylvester), and is \emph{mixed} when $p, q \geq 1$.

The \emph{Clifford algebra} $\Cl(p,q) = \Cl(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is generated by $\mathbb{V}$ subject to $v^2 = Q(v)$. Polarising gives $ab + ba = 2\,a \cdot b$, so orthogonal vectors anticommute; $ab = a \cdot b + a \wedge b$ with $a \wedge b \mathrel{:=} \tfrac12(ab-ba)$ the \emph{outer product}, pure grade two. The ordered products $e_{i_1} \cdots e_{i_k}$ over an orthogonal basis, $i_1 < \dots < i_k$, the \emph{basis blades} with $1$ as the empty product, form a linear basis, so $\dim \Cl(\mathbb{V},Q) = 2^n$; this holds for degenerate forms too \cite{Chevalley1997}, which we need once (Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane}). An element has \emph{grade} $k$ if it combines blades of length $k$, basis-independently \cite{Porteous1995}. A vector with $Q(v) \neq 0$ is invertible, $v^{-1} = v/Q(v)$; a nonzero vector with $Q(v) = 0$ is \emph{null}, and null vectors exist exactly in mixed signature, where they form a cone \cite[Sections 2 to 4]{ButlerT0}. A word on the two notations: we write $\Cl(p,q)$ whenever only the signature matters, and $\Cl(\mathbb{V})$ or $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ for the algebra of a \emph{specific} quadratic space, chiefly an extension quantified over in a theorem, whose form is not assumed nondegenerate and so may carry no signature label at all.

t01-regenerated.title: Null vectors, zero divisors, and hyperbolic planes
t01-regenerated.text:
Null vectors are moreover two-sided zero divisors. The obstruction they pose is packaged in the reciprocal map
\[
\rho : \mathbb{V} \setminus \{Q = 0\} \to \mathbb{V}, \qquad \rho(x) = x / Q(x),
\]
which is partial exactly on $\{Q = 0\}$, the null cone together with the origin. Both failure modes are resolved by the same completion (Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}); only the null cone poses the element-level question of the section ``The refuted conjecture, and the no-go'', the pseudo-inverse condition being vacuous at the origin.

Null vectors come in pairs. If $v$ is null and $Q$ is nondegenerate, there is a vector $a$ with $v \cdot a \neq 0$; rescaling so that $v \cdot a = \tfrac12$ and setting $w = a - Q(a)\,v$ gives
\[
Q(w) = Q(a) - 2\,Q(a)\,(v \cdot a) = 0, \qquad v \cdot w = v \cdot a = \tfrac12 :
\]
a \emph{hyperbolic pair} $(v, w)$. The plane $H = \mathrm{span}\{v, w\}$ is a \emph{hyperbolic plane}: its Gram matrix on $(v,w)$ has determinant $-\tfrac14$, so $H$ is nondegenerate of signature $(1,1)$, and conversely every two-dimensional nondegenerate space containing a null vector is isometric to $H$ \cite{Lam2005}. Inside the Clifford algebra a hyperbolic pair satisfies
\begin{equation}
v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v .
\end{equation}
The last identity says $w$ is a \emph{pseudo-inverse} of $v$ in the sense of von Neumann: division by $v$ cannot be undone exactly, but $w$ undoes it up to the defect of $v$. This is the weakened form of inversion around which the section ``The refuted conjecture, and the no-go'' revolves.

Fix a null $v \in \Ncone$ and a null partner $w_0$ with $v \cdot w_0 = \tfrac12$, by the hyperbolic-pair construction of the section ``Null vectors, zero divisors, and hyperbolic planes'' (\claimref{std-algebra.witt-decomposition}); write $H_0 = \mathrm{span}\{v, w_0\}$ and $U = \{v, w_0\}^{\perp} \cap \mathbb{V}$, a nondegenerate subspace of $\mathbb{V}$ of dimension $n - 2 \geq 1$. By Definition \claimref{obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces} the extension splits as $\mathbb{V}' = \mathbb{V} \perp \mathbb{V}^{\perp}$, so
\[
\mathbb{V}' \;=\; H_0 \perp U', \qquad U' \mathrel{:=} U \perp \mathbb{V}^{\perp},
\]
and Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane} applies: every candidate $\sigma = \sigma(v) \in \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ has a unique expansion $\sigma = \alpha + v\beta + w_0\gamma + v w_0 \delta$ with $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Cl(U')$. Throughout, $\hat{\cdot}$ is the grade involution and we use the commutation rule $v\,x = \hat{x}\,v, \qquad x\,v = v\,\hat{x}$ (Lemma \claimref{primer.commutation-rule}) for $v$ against $\Cl(U')$, together with the hyperbolic-pair identities $v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v$.

\emph{Step 1 (normal form for pseudo-inverses).} Compute $v\sigma v$ term by term:
\[
v\,\alpha\, v = v\, (\alpha v) = v\,(v \hat{\alpha}) = v^2 \hat\alpha = 0, \qquad
v\,(v\beta)\,v = v^2 \beta v = 0, \qquad
v\,(v w_0 \delta)\,v = v^2 w_0 \delta v = 0,
\]
while the third term survives:
\[
v\,(w_0 \gamma)\,v \;=\; v w_0\,(\gamma v) \;=\; v w_0\, v \hat{\gamma} \;=\; v \hat{\gamma}
\]
by $v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v$. Hence $v \sigma v = v \hat{\gamma}$, and since left multiplication by $v$ is injective on $\Cl(U')$ (Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane}(2)) and $\hat{\cdot}$ is an involution, $v \sigma v = v$ holds if and only if $\gamma = 1$. Every pseudo-inverse of $v$ therefore has the form
\[
\sigma \;=\; w_0 + \alpha + v\beta + v w_0 \delta .
\]

\emph{Step 2 (null rotations).} For $u \in U$ set $R = 1 + vu$. Since $v \cdot u = 0$ and $v^2 = 0$,
\[
(vu)^2 = v\,(uv)\,u = -v\,(vu)\,u = -v^2 u^2 = 0, \qquad \text{and in particular} \quad vuv = -v^2u = 0,
\]
so $R = \exp(vu) = \exp(v \wedge u)$, with $R^{-1} = 1 - vu$. $R$ is even, and its reverse is $\widetilde{R} = 1 + uv = 1 - vu = R^{-1}$, so $R \widetilde{R} = 1$ and $R$ is a rotor.

Take from now on $u$ with $Q(u) \neq 0$, which is possible because $U$ is nondegenerate and nonzero; such $u$ span $U$. Then $R$ is a versor outright, not merely a rotor. Indeed the vector $u' \mathrel{:=} u + Q(u)\,v$ satisfies $Q(u') = Q(u) + 2Q(u)\,(u \cdot v) = Q(u) \neq 0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:versorfactor}
u'u \;=\; u^2 + Q(u)\,vu \;=\; Q(u)\,(1 + vu), \qquad \text{so} \qquad R \;=\; \frac{u'\,u}{Q(u)},
\end{equation}

Hence $R \in \Spin(p,q)$. The same factorisation applies with $u$ replaced by $tu$ for every $t \neq 0$, so $t \mapsto 1 + t\,vu$ is a continuous path \emph{inside the group} joining $1$ to $R$, and therefore $R \in \Spin^0(p,q)$.

Its action on vectors is computed directly. On $v$:
\[
R\,v\,R^{-1} = (1 + vu)\,v\,(1 - vu) = (v + vuv)(1 - vu) = v(1 - vu) = v - v^2u = v ,
\]
so $R$ fixes $v$. On $u'' \in U'$, using $u''v = -vu''$, $u u'' v = v u u''$ (two anticommutations) and $vuv = 0$:
\[
R\,u''\,R^{-1} = u'' - u''vu + vuu'' - vuu''vu = u'' + v(u''u + uu'') - v(vuu'')u = u'' + 2(u \cdot u'')\,v .
\]
On $w_0$, using $w_0 v = 1 - v w_0$ and $u w_0 = -w_0 u$:
\[
vuw_0 - w_0vu = -vw_0u - (1 - vw_0)u = -u, \qquad
vuw_0vu = vu(1 - vw_0)u = vu^2 - (vuv)w_0u = Q(u)\,v,
\]
whence
\[
R\,w_0\,R^{-1} = w_0 + (vuw_0 - w_0vu) - vuw_0vu = w_0 - u - Q(u)\,v .
\]

\begin{align*}
R\,\alpha\,R^{-1} &= \alpha + vu\alpha - \alpha vu - vu\alpha vu
= \alpha + v\,(u\alpha - \hat{\alpha}u) && (\alpha vu = v\hat\alpha u;\ vu\alpha v = vuv\hat\alpha = 0),\\
R\,(v\beta)\,R^{-1} &= v\beta + (vuv)\beta - (v\beta v)u - (vuv)\beta vu = v\beta && (v\beta v = v^2\hat\beta = 0),\\
R\,(v w_0 \delta)\,R^{-1} &= v w_0 \delta - v w_0 \delta v u = v w_0 \delta - v\hat{\delta}u && (v w_0 \delta v u = v w_0 v \hat{\delta} u = v \hat\delta u),\\
R\,w_0\,R^{-1} &= w_0 - u - Q(u)\,v && \text{(Step 2)}.
\end{align*}

deposited.statement: Let $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ be nondegenerate of mixed signature $(p,q)$, $p, q \geq 1$, with $n = p + q \geq 3$, and let $\Ncone \subset \mathbb{V}$ be its null cone. Let $(\mathbb{V}', Q')$ be \emph{any} extension of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ in the sense of Definition 2.3, possibly $\mathbb{V}$ itself. Then there is no map $\sigma : \Ncone \to \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ satisfying $v\,\sigma(v)\,v = v$ for every null $v$ that is equivariant, in the sense of Definition 2.2, even under the identity component $\Spin^0(p,q)$; a fortiori none equivariant under $\Spin(p,q)$ or $\Pin(p,q)$. Equivariant division by zero is impossible at the level of elements, in the Clifford algebra of every ascent, however large.
deposited.proof:
Fix a null $v \in \Ncone$ and a null partner $w_0$ with $v \cdot w_0 = \tfrac12$, by the hyperbolic-pair construction of Section 2.2; write $H_0 = \mathrm{span}\{v, w_0\}$ and $U = \{v, w_0\}^{\perp} \cap \mathbb{V}$, a nondegenerate subspace of $\mathbb{V}$ of dimension $n - 2 \geq 1$. By Definition 2.3 the extension splits as $\mathbb{V}' = \mathbb{V} \perp \mathbb{V}^{\perp}$, so
\[
\mathbb{V}' \;=\; H_0 \perp U', \qquad U' \mathrel{:=} U \perp \mathbb{V}^{\perp},
\]
and Lemma 2.4 applies: every candidate $\sigma = \sigma(v) \in \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ has a unique expansion $\sigma = \alpha + v\beta + w_0\gamma + v w_0 \delta$ with $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Cl(U')$. Throughout, $\hat{\cdot}$ is the grade involution and we use the commutation rule (1) for $v$ against $\Cl(U')$, together with the hyperbolic-pair identities (2).

\emph{Step 1 (normal form for pseudo-inverses).} Compute $v\sigma v$ term by term:
\[
v\,\alpha\, v = v\, (\alpha v) = v\,(v \hat{\alpha}) = v^2 \hat\alpha = 0, \qquad
v\,(v\beta)\,v = v^2 \beta v = 0, \qquad
v\,(v w_0 \delta)\,v = v^2 w_0 \delta v = 0,
\]
while the third term survives:
\[
v\,(w_0 \gamma)\,v \;=\; v w_0\,(\gamma v) \;=\; v w_0\, v \hat{\gamma} \;=\; v \hat{\gamma}
\]
by (2). Hence $v \sigma v = v \hat{\gamma}$, and since left multiplication by $v$ is injective on $\Cl(U')$ (Lemma 2.4(2)) and $\hat{\cdot}$ is an involution, $v \sigma v = v$ holds if and only if $\gamma = 1$. Every pseudo-inverse of $v$ therefore has the form
\[
\sigma \;=\; w_0 + \alpha + v\beta + v w_0 \delta .
\]
Note that only the first von Neumann identity is used; the theorem does not even require $\sigma v \sigma = \sigma$.

\emph{Step 2 (null rotations).} For $u \in U$ set $R = 1 + vu$. Since $v \cdot u = 0$ and $v^2 = 0$,
\[
(vu)^2 = v\,(uv)\,u = -v\,(vu)\,u = -v^2 u^2 = 0, \qquad \text{and in particular} \quad vuv = -v^2u = 0,
\]
so $R = \exp(vu) = \exp(v \wedge u)$, with $R^{-1} = 1 - vu$. $R$ is even, and its reverse is $\widetilde{R} = 1 + uv = 1 - vu = R^{-1}$, so $R \widetilde{R} = 1$ and $R$ is a rotor.

Take from now on $u$ with $Q(u) \neq 0$, which is possible because $U$ is nondegenerate and nonzero; such $u$ span $U$. Then $R$ is a versor outright, not merely a rotor. Indeed the vector $u' \mathrel{:=} u + Q(u)\,v$ satisfies $Q(u') = Q(u) + 2Q(u)\,(u \cdot v) = Q(u) \neq 0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:versorfactor}
u'u \;=\; u^2 + Q(u)\,vu \;=\; Q(u)\,(1 + vu), \qquad \text{so} \qquad R \;=\; \frac{u'\,u}{Q(u)},
\end{equation}
a product of two invertible vectors of equal square. Normalising both factors to unit square multiplies the product by $|Q(u)|/Q(u) = \pm 1$, and when that sign is $-1$ we have $Q(u) < 0$, so the normalised $\hat{u} = u/\sqrt{|Q(u)|}$ satisfies $\hat{u}^2 = -1$ and the sign is itself a product of unit vectors. Hence $R \in \Spin(p,q)$. The same factorisation applies with $u$ replaced by $tu$ for every $t \neq 0$, so $t \mapsto 1 + t\,vu$ is a continuous path \emph{inside the group} joining $1$ to $R$, and therefore $R \in \Spin^0(p,q)$.

Its action on vectors is computed directly. On $v$:
\[
R\,v\,R^{-1} = (1 + vu)\,v\,(1 - vu) = (v + vuv)(1 - vu) = v(1 - vu) = v - v^2u = v ,
\]
so $R$ fixes $v$. On $u'' \in U'$, using $u''v = -vu''$, $u u'' v = v u u''$ (two anticommutations) and $vuv = 0$:
\[
R\,u''\,R^{-1} = u'' - u''vu + vuu'' - vuu''vu = u'' + v(u''u + uu'') - v(vuu'')u = u'' + 2(u \cdot u'')\,v .
\]
On $w_0$, using $w_0 v = 1 - v w_0$ and $u w_0 = -w_0 u$:
\[
vuw_0 - w_0vu = -vw_0u - (1 - vw_0)u = -u, \qquad
vuw_0vu = vu(1 - vw_0)u = vu^2 - (vuv)w_0u = Q(u)\,v,
\]
whence
\[
R\,w_0\,R^{-1} = w_0 + (vuw_0 - w_0vu) - vuw_0vu = w_0 - u - Q(u)\,v .
\]
These are the \emph{null rotations}, the parabolic transvections stabilising the null direction $v$.

\emph{Step 3 (the shear).} Conjugate the normal form of Step 1 by $R$ and collect the $\Cl(U')$-component, i.e.\ the coefficient of $1 \in \Cl(H_0)$ in the unique expansion of Lemma 2.4. Term by term, using $\alpha v = v\hat\alpha$, $\delta v = v \hat\delta$, $\beta v = v\hat\beta$ and $vuv = 0$:
\begin{align*}
R\,\alpha\,R^{-1} &= \alpha + vu\alpha - \alpha vu - vu\alpha vu
= \alpha + v\,(u\alpha - \hat{\alpha}u) && (\alpha vu = v\hat\alpha u;\ vu\alpha v = vuv\hat\alpha = 0),\\
R\,(v\beta)\,R^{-1} &= v\beta + (vuv)\beta - (v\beta v)u - (vuv)\beta vu = v\beta && (v\beta v = v^2\hat\beta = 0),\\
R\,(v w_0 \delta)\,R^{-1} &= v w_0 \delta - v w_0 \delta v u = v w_0 \delta - v\hat{\delta}u && (v w_0 \delta v u = v w_0 v \hat{\delta} u = v \hat\delta u),\\
R\,w_0\,R^{-1} &= w_0 - u - Q(u)\,v && \text{(Step 2)}.
\end{align*}
Every correction except one retains a left factor of $v$ and therefore lies in the $v$- or $vw_0$-slots of the expansion; the sole contribution to the $\Cl(U')$-component comes from $R w_0 R^{-1}$, and that component of $R\,\sigma(v)\,R^{-1}$ equals $\alpha - u$. But $R$ fixes $v$, so equivariance demands $\tau_R(\sigma(v)) = R\,\sigma(v)\,R^{-1} = \sigma(v)$; comparing $\Cl(U')$-components in the unique expansion gives $\alpha - u = \alpha$, i.e.\ $u = 0$, for \emph{every} $u \in U$ with $Q(u) \neq 0$. Since $U$ is nondegenerate of dimension $n - 2 \geq 1$, such $u$ exist, a contradiction.

t01-regenerated.title: Locality and robustness of the obstruction
t01-regenerated.text:
The proof consumes far less than the theorem's hypotheses offer, and it is worth recording what it actually uses, since the surplus rules out the obvious weakenings.

\emph{It is local.} Only the stabiliser of a \emph{single} null vector enters. The sharp statement proved above is therefore: \emph{for one null vector $v$ there is no $\sigma \in \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ with $v\sigma v = v$ that is invariant under the null rotations fixing $v$.} No global rule, no coherence across the cone, and no regularity of $\sigma$ (continuity, measurability, genericity) is assumed or would help; the theorem as stated follows at once.

\emph{It survives equivariance up to scale.} The natural first weakening is to ask only that $\sigma(v)$ be canonical projectively, $\tau_R(\sigma(v)) = \lambda\,\sigma(v)$ for some $\lambda \neq 0$. This fails too. In the normal form of Step 1 the $w_0$-coefficient is $\gamma = 1$, and Step 3 shows it is unchanged by conjugation; comparing $w_0$-components forces $\lambda = 1$, whereupon the $\Cl(U')$-comparison gives the same contradiction $u = 0$.

t01-regenerated.title: The obstruction is parabolic
t01-regenerated.text: The stabiliser of a null direction in an indefinite orthogonal group is not \emph{reductive}: it contains a nontrivial normal subgroup of \emph{unipotent} elements, transformations $g$ for which $g - \mathrm{id}$ is nilpotent (here $(R-1)^2 = 0$ in the algebra, while on $\mathbb{V}$ the action satisfies $(\Ad_R - \mathrm{id})^3 = 0$, with $(\Ad_R - \mathrm{id})^2 w_0 = -2Q(u)\,v$ nonzero whenever $Q(u) \neq 0$), called its unipotent radical. (``Parabolic'' parallels the M\"obius classification: like a parabolic M\"obius map, a null rotation is unipotent and fixes the null direction $[v]$; for $n = 3$ it fixes no other direction at all, while for $n \geq 4$ it fixes in addition the subspace $U \cap u^{\perp}$, which may itself contain null directions.) Step 3 shows that this radical acts on the candidate partners by translating the $\Cl(U')$-coefficient $\alpha$ by $-u$, freely and without fixed point; Proposition \claimref{transport.pseudo-inverse-torsor} makes that action exact. First, enlarging the algebra can never help: the shearing rotors $R = 1 + vu$ and the translation vectors $u$ lie inside $\Cl(\mathbb{V})$ and act the same way in every extension, which is why Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} quantifies over all ascents at once. The quantifier ranges over the Clifford algebra of an extension quadratic space (Definition \claimref{obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces}), which is what the splitting of Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane} requires; it extends verbatim to matrix algebras $M_k\bigl(\Cl(\mathbb{V}')\bigr)$ over such an algebra, since reading $v\sigma v = v$ entrywise, with $v$ embedded as $v\,I$, makes each diagonal entry of $\sigma$ an invariant pseudo-inverse in $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ and so contradicts the theorem. Second, the phenomenon is absent in definite signature, where there are no null vectors and stabilisers of directions are compact and reductive: it is a genuinely mixed-signature obstruction, present exactly where the null cone is.

t01-regenerated.title: The hyperbolic atom
t01-regenerated.text:
The assumption $n \geq 3$ is necessary, and the bound is sharp. For $n = 2$ the space is itself a hyperbolic plane, $U = 0$, there are no null rotations, and the assignment $\sigma(\lambda v) = \lambda^{-1} w_0$, $\sigma(\lambda w_0) = \lambda^{-1} v$ defines a genuinely $\Pin(1,1)$-equivariant pseudo-inverse section in the sense of Definition \claimref{obj.transport.equivariance}, and no ascent is needed: the hyperbolic plane is self-complete \emph{at the level of elements}. (Its reciprocal on \emph{points} is of course still partial; Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} applies to it like any other base, and its own transport is $\Cl(2,2)$. The two senses of completion are exactly the two halves of the transport principle, and the atom separates them.)

The section has a coordinate-free description, which is the real reason for its equivariance and simultaneously explains the failure for $n \geq 3$. For null $x$, call $y$ a \emph{partner} of $x$ if $y$ is null with $x \cdot y = \tfrac12$. Writing $y = av + bw_0 + u$ with $u \in U$, the two conditions read $b = 1$ and $a = -Q(u)$, so the partners of $v$ are exactly
\begin{equation}
y_u \;=\; w_0 - u - Q(u)\,v \qquad (u \in U),
\end{equation}
an affine space of dimension $n - 2$ on which, by Step 2 of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, the null rotations act simply transitively. For $n = 2$ it is a single point, so ``the partner of $x$'' is a well-formed metric description and $\sigma$ is equivariant for that reason alone, with no computation; for $n \geq 3$ a torsor has no distinguished point, and Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} says no enlargement of the space produces one. This is precisely why the hyperbolic plane is the unit of transport: the ascent of the section ``The completion: the conformal model'' adjoins a copy of the one quadratic space that needs no ascent of the first kind.


The same dimension count is Zeeman's. By Zeeman's theorem \cite{Zeeman1964}, for $n \geq 3$ every bijection of Minkowski space preserving the causal order is generated by Lorentz transformations, translations and dilations, while in $n = 2$ the two null coordinates can be reparametrised independently and the causal automorphism group is infinite-dimensional. The two-dimensional counterexamples to Zeeman are exactly the freedom that the null rotations remove for $n \geq 3$ by mixing each null direction with the transverse ones; the little group of a null direction has a null-rotation part of dimension $n - 2$, and both theorems hold precisely when it is present. Zeeman's theorem is imported here, not proved, and nothing below depends on it; this paragraph records that the third hypothesis of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} and Zeeman's are the same hypothesis, the existence of a null rotation, so that the hyperbolic atom is the exception to both for one reason.

\[
N_v \;=\; \{\, R_u : u \in U \,\}
\]
is an abelian subgroup of $\Spin^0(p,q)$, and $u \mapsto R_u$ is an isomorphism of groups $(U, +) \cong N_v$. Each $R_u$ fixes $v$. Moreover the assignment is equivariant for the Levi factor: every rotor $g$ in the even subalgebra of $\Cl(U)$ fixes $v$ and satisfies $g\, R_u\, g^{-1} = R_{g u g^{-1}}$, the conjugation on the right being the vector action of $\Spin(U)$ on $U$.

On $S(v)$ define $\sigma \sim \sigma'$ iff $\sigma - \sigma' \in v\,\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$, the left ideal generated by $v$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Each class contains a unique representative of the form $w_0 + \alpha$ with $\alpha \in \Cl(U')$, so the quotient $T(v) := S(v)/\!\sim$ is an affine space with translation space $\Cl(U')$, via $[w_0 + \alpha] + \xi = [w_0 + \alpha + \xi]$.
\item $N_v$ preserves $S(v)$ and the equivalence, hence acts on $T(v)$; the action is by translations along the grade-one subspace $U \subseteq \Cl(U')$:
\[
R_u \cdot [\,w_0 + \alpha\,] \;=\; [\,w_0 + \alpha - u\,].
\]
\item The $N_v$-orbit of any class is a torsor under $(U, +)$, and its translation cocycle, with respect to any base point, is the tautological homomorphism $\theta : N_v \to U$, $\theta(R_u) = u$.
\end{enumerate}

t01-regenerated.title: The completion: the conformal model
t01-regenerated.text:
This section is standard \cite{Hestenes2001, HLR2001, DFM2007, DoranLasenby2003}; we fix conventions and, for later use, the topology. Adjoin to $\mathbb{V}$ two orthogonal directions $e_+, e_-$ with $e_+^2 = 1$, $e_-^2 = -1$, both orthogonal to $\mathbb{V}$, giving $\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$. Define the null pair
\[
\nO = \tfrac12(e_- - e_+), \qquad \nInf = e_- + e_+,
\]
so that $\nO^2 = \nInf^2 = 0$ and $\nO \cdot \nInf = -1$; the plane $H = \mathrm{span}\{\nO, \nInf\}$ they span is hyperbolic (the section ``Null vectors, zero divisors, and hyperbolic planes''). Represent each point $x \in \mathbb{V}$ by
\begin{equation}
X(x) \;=\; \nO + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\, \nInf .
\end{equation}
Direct computation gives the two standard identities
\begin{equation}
X(x)^2 = 0, \qquad X(x)\cdot X(y) = -\tfrac12\, Q(x-y),
\end{equation}
so every point is represented by a null vector, and the representation is metrically faithful. Representatives are regarded projectively: a \emph{point} of the model is a null ray $[\,X\,] = \{\lambda X : \lambda \in \R^\times\}$ on the quadric
\[
\mathcal{Q} \;=\; \{[N] : N \in \mathbb{V} \oplus H,\ N \neq 0,\ N^2 = 0\}
\]
of the ambient space. Writing a general vector as $N = s\,\nO + x + t\,\nInf$ ($s, t \in \R$, $x \in \mathbb{V}$), one has $N \cdot \nInf = -s$; the rays with $s = 0$, an invariant condition since it reads $N \cdot \nInf = 0$, are not of the form $[X(x)]$ for any $x$, and we call them \emph{ideal points}. As is well known, the versor group of $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ acting by the relation displayed with \claimref{transport.noinverse} realises on $\mathcal{Q}$ the full conformal group of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$, the group of its angle-preserving transformations, with inversions realised by reflections \cite{HLR2001, Angles2008}.

t01-regenerated.title: Minimality
t01-regenerated.text:
Let $(\mathbb{W}, f)$ be any null-lift completion of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$. Then $\mathbb{W}$ contains at least one direction of positive square and one of negative square; in particular $\dim \mathbb{W} \geq 2$, and enlargements of signature increment $(+k, 0)$ or $(0, +k)$ are excluded for every $k$. A single hyperbolic plane suffices, and any two-dimensional $\mathbb{W}$ admitted by the definition is a hyperbolic plane; hence the minimal completion is
\[
\Cl(p,q) \;\longrightarrow\; \Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1),
\]
with the adjoined space unique up to isometry, and the signature increment is $(+1,+1)$ in every signature.

\]

(When $\mathbb{V}$ has mixed signature the same conclusion follows a second way, with no appeal to the origin: $-Q$ attains both signs, hence so does $Q_{\mathbb{W}}$.)

For uniqueness of the minimal $\mathbb{W}$: a two-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space containing a nonzero null vector is indefinite, hence of signature $(1,1)$, and is the hyperbolic plane, unique up to isometry (the section ``Null vectors, zero divisors, and hyperbolic planes'', \cite{Lam2005}; \claimref{std-algebra.sylvester-inertia}). t01-regenerated.title: Remark on Minimality
t01-regenerated.text: Two small arguments carry the theorem, and they deserve emphasis for how little they assume. The no-go theorem requires $p, q \geq 1$ and $n \geq 3$ and does not apply here, since with no null vectors there is no element-level question to obstruct, while the theorems this example exercises (totality, minimality, the normal form) hold in every nondegenerate signature, as recorded in the scope paragraph of the section ``Quadratic spaces and Clifford algebras''.

\[

\[
\iota[X(z)] = [X(z/|z|^2)] \ \ (z \neq 0), \qquad \iota[X(0)] = [\nInf], \qquad \iota[\nInf] = [X(0)],
\]
and $z \mapsto z/|z|^2 = 1/\bar{z}$ is inversion in the unit circle. On the sphere it is the reflection
\[
(X, Y, Z) \;\mapsto\; (X, Y, -Z)
\]

The algebra $\Cl(1,1)$ is isomorphic to the algebra $M_2(\R)$ of real $2 \times 2$ matrices: with $e_0^2 = 1$, $e_1^2 = -1$, the assignment
\[
e_0 \mapsto E = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, \qquad
e_1 \mapsto F = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}
\]
satisfies $E^2 = I$, $F^2 = -I$ and $EF + FE = 0$, hence extends to an algebra isomorphism (both algebras have dimension four; $M_2(\R)$ is simple). A base vector $x e_0 + y e_1$ maps to $\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & x+y \\ x-y & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$, of determinant $-(x^2 - y^2) = -Q$: \emph{a vector is null exactly when its matrix is singular}. In particular the hyperbolic pair $v = \tfrac12(e_0 + e_1)$, $w_0 = \tfrac12(e_0 - e_1)$ (so $v \cdot w_0 = \tfrac12$) maps to
\[
v \;\mapsto\; N = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, \qquad
w_0 \;\mapsto\; N^{\mathsf T} = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}.
\]
Under this dictionary the objects of the section ``The refuted conjecture, and the no-go'' become textbook objects of linear algebra: the equation $v\,\sigma(v)\,v = v$ is Penrose's first equation $AXA = A$ for a \emph{generalized inverse} of a singular matrix, and the abundance of pseudo-inverses noted there is the familiar abundance of generalized inverses.

Matrix theory has a canonical selection among them: the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse $A^{+}$, which for a rank-one matrix is $A^{+} = A^{\mathsf T}/\lVert A \rVert_F^{\,2}$. Applied to the null vectors of this base,
\[
(\lambda N)^{+} = \lambda^{-1} N^{\mathsf T}, \qquad (\lambda N^{\mathsf T})^{+} = \lambda^{-1} N,
\]
which is, under the isomorphism, \emph{exactly} the equivariant section $\sigma(\lambda v) = \lambda^{-1} w_0$, $\sigma(\lambda w_0) = \lambda^{-1} v$ of Remark \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom}: the hyperbolic atom's self-completeness is the Moore--Penrose construction expressed in the Clifford algebra. The agreement is not a coincidence of formulas. By \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom} the partner of a null vector in a hyperbolic plane is unique, so any rule at all that returns a null partner returns this one; the Euclidean transpose supplies it, and so does the metric description.

The agreement extends to the failure, which is the instructive part. It is classical that $A^{+}$ is canonical only relative to a choice of \emph{definite} inner product: it is built from the transpose, the adjoint of the Euclidean metric, and transforms correctly under orthogonal maps, $(UAV)^{+} = V^{\mathsf T} A^{+}\, U^{\mathsf T}$ for orthogonal $U, V$, but not under general invertible ones. Known theory therefore already signals that the obvious candidate for $\sigma$ must fail to respect an \emph{indefinite} symmetry group, which preserves no definite inner product. Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} is the sharp form of that signal. For $n = 2$ the stabiliser of a null direction in $O(1,1)$ contains no null rotations, nothing shears, the partner set \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom} is a single point, and the Moore--Penrose choice survives as an equivariant section (Remark \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom}). The no-go theorem thus marks the precise boundary of the Moore--Penrose phenomenon: canonical generalized inversion of null directions ends exactly where parabolic stabilisers begin.

\[

\]

So $W \cong V_+^{\,a} \oplus V_-^{\,b}$ as an $A$-module with $a, b \geq 1$ and
\[
md \;=\; (a + b)\,k f \;\geq\; 2kf .
\]
Moreover the right $D$-action on $W$ commutes with $A$, so $D$ embeds unitally in the commutant (strictly, the right action embeds $D^{\mathrm{op}}$; harmless, as $\R$, $\C$ and $\HH$ are each isomorphic to their opposites, and the dimension bounds below are opposite-invariant) $\mathrm{End}_A(W) \cong \Mat_a(\mathbb{F}) \oplus \Mat_b(\mathbb{F})$ (using $\mathrm{End}_{\Mat_k(\mathbb{F})}(\mathbb{F}^k) \cong \mathbb{F}$ as real algebras), hence, projecting to each summand, unitally in both $\Mat_a(\mathbb{F})$ and $\Mat_b(\mathbb{F})$.

\]
satisfies both von Neumann identities, $e\,\sigma(e)\,e = e$ and $\sigma(e)\,e\,\sigma(e) = \sigma(e)$, and is equivariant under \emph{every} ring automorphism of every extension: for any automorphism $\theta$ of $A'$ preserving $A$, $\sigma(\theta(e)) = \theta(\sigma(e))$ trivially. t01-regenerated.text:
Define the pinching $E : B \to B$, $E(x) = PxP + (1-P)x(1-P)$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $E$ is an idempotent linear map whose image is the commutant $C = \{x \in B : xP = Px\} = A \oplus A\,ff^*$, on which it restricts to the identity, and $E$ is a $C$-bimodule map: $E(cxc') = c\,E(x)\,c'$ for $c, c' \in C$, with $E(1) = 1$: a conditional expectation onto $C$.
\item Its kernel is exactly the adjoined ladder sector:
\[
\ker E \;=\; PB(1-P) \,\oplus\, (1-P)BP \;=\; A f^* \,\oplus\, A f .
\]
In particular $E(f) = E(f^*) = 0$: the pinching erases precisely the pair the ascent adjoined, and nothing else.
\item The round trip is exact on transported elements: for $a \in A$, $E(a) = a$, and the corner read-out $D(x) = PxP$, identified with an $A$-valued map through the natural corner isomorphism $E_{22}BE_{22} = A\,f^*f \cong A$ ($a \mapsto a\,f^*f$), satisfies $D(a) = a$: ascent-then-descent is the \emph{identity} on the base. (In the Peirce coordinates of Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}, which identify the $(2,2)$ block with the $(1,1)$ corner by conjugating with $E_{12} = f$, the same round trip reads as the grade involution $\hat{a}$; the two corner identifications differ by exactly the grade twist of the embedding $a \mapsto \mathrm{diag}(a,\hat a)$, and either way the map is an automorphism, faithful.) The multiplicative defect of $D$ on general elements is the exact interposition formula
\[
D(xy) - D(x)D(y) \;=\; P\,x\,(1-P)\,y\,P .
\]
\end{enumerate}

t01-regenerated.title: The transport principle, and the algorithm
t01-regenerated.text:
The Principle is a summary, not an axiom: each of its clauses is one of the theorems proved above, and it adds nothing to them. What it does add is the reading. The three costs are not a graded scale of difficulty but three different answers to one equivariance question, and the question is answerable at all only because the taxonomy is exhaustive: it is the completeness of Theorem \claimref{transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent}, not the ingenuity of any rule, that turns a family of repairs into a procedure.

Two closing observations. First, the shape of the type-N answer is the surprising one, and it is worth stating plainly that it is a change of level rather than a technical fix: what is repaired is not the element, which remains non-invertible in every enlargement however large, but the space in which the element's division was asked. Second, no transport removes all obstructions. Every completion carries obstructions of its own, and in the type-N case the adjoined pair is itself null (Proposition \claimref{transport.no-transport-terminates}): the repair of the old null cone is effected by adjoining new members of it. What the bookkeeping of the section ``The mod-8 clock and the one-way door'' shows is therefore not that transport terminates but that it stabilises, the clock moving at most once and then remaining fixed. Obstruction is conserved; what the rules achieve is that it no longer changes the Wedderburn type.

The paper is intended to be independently checkable throughout: every algebraic statement can be verified from the axiom $v^2 = Q(v)$ with pencil and paper, the topological statements of the section ``Totality of the transported reciprocal'' from the elementary point-set facts recorded in the section ``The completion: the conformal model'', and every computational identity by the deposited scripts.

t01-regenerated.title: The transport algorithm
t01-regenerated.text:
The Principle says what is true; practice needs to know what to do. The theorems distil into a six-step procedure, and every step names the theorem, proved above, that licenses it. the table accompanying \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm} is the one-page version: the theorems in operational form. That the steps form a decision procedure with no gaps is itself a theorem, Corollary \claimref{transport.no-fourth-rule}.




\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textbf{Step 1.}] \textbf{Locate the failure.} Identify the element at which invertibility fails, or, if the construction is a family, the locus at which it fails. Nothing later depends on how this is done; it is a computation in the case at hand. What the algebra guarantees is that the failure cannot be argued away: a null vector has no inverse in \emph{any} unital algebra containing the base (Lemma \claimref{transport.noinverse}), and neither has an idempotent.

\item[\textbf{Step 2.}] \textbf{Diagnose the type.} Ask, in order:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Is the failing element a vector $v$ with $Q(v) = 0$? Then the obstruction is \textbf{type N}. These exist exactly in mixed signature, $pq \neq 0$ (Proposition \claimref{transport.existence-locus-type-n}).
  \item Is it a \emph{central} idempotent? Then \textbf{type C}. These exist exactly when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and are then exactly the two projectors $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega)$ (Theorem \claimref{transport.existence-classification-type-c}); equivalently, exactly when the algebra is not simple (Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}).

In brief: T2 \cite{ButlerT2} takes the element-level lemma that a square-zero element is invertible in no unital extension (Lemma \claimref{transport.noinverse}), the type-N reading of a radical direction with the taxonomy frame, and the scope of the sharpenings of the section ``Minimality against arbitrary embeddings'', and proves its own completion theorem for degenerate algebras against that frame; T3 \cite{ButlerT3} iterates Rule 1 into the tower, using the Morita theorem and the pinching; T4 \cite{ButlerT4} localises the taxonomy and Rule 1 over degenerate loci, using the splitting lemma and the null-generator clause of Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified}; T5 \cite{ButlerT5} runs the whole algorithm on the black-hole singularity, importing the no-go, totality, minimality, the type-C exclusion for $\Cl(1,3)$, the pinching, and the one-way door; and the papers after T5 \cite{ButlerT5} import these results through T3 \cite{ButlerT3}, T4 \cite{ButlerT4} and T5 \cite{ButlerT5} rather than directly, with each paper's Fact environments carrying the exact provenance. The capstone T17 \cite{ButlerT17} maps the series and records the status of every claim.

One subsection points forward without relying on anything: the sentence after Corollary \claimref{transport.which-residues-obstruct-which-way} names the dark-matter paper T14 \cite{ButlerT14} for the residues $\{2, 6\}$. It is a pointer, and the theorems of the section ``One-dimensional extensions: where the obstruction lies, and the commuting square'' use only this paper.

t01-regenerated.text:
Every computational identity in this paper has been checked by computer in exact rational arithmetic. The consolidated script \texttt{verify\_T01.py} \cite{ButlerVerifyT01}, deposited alongside the series' shared exact-arithmetic library \texttt{GA.py}, runs one hundred and fifteen checks and reports each; no floating point is used anywhere except the Moore--Penrose comparisons of the section ``The hyperbolic atom as a matrix algebra: the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse'', which are float and compared at machine precision, and the script exits nonzero on any failure.

The twenty-two checks inherited from the published deposit's script cover: the hyperbolic-pair and versor identities; Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane}, including over an extension carrying a degenerate direction, where the dimension count is the essential step; all three steps of the proof of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} in $\Cl(2,1)$ and in $\Cl(3,2)$, the latter exercising the shear for \emph{every} $u$ in a three-dimensional $U$; the scale-robustness of Remark \claimref{note.transport.locality-robustness-obstruction}, the nilpotency data of Remark \claimref{note.transport.obstruction-parabolic}, and the partner parametrisation \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom} with the simple transitivity on it; both branches of Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} and the limit paths of Lemma \claimref{transport.density} over bases of signature $(1,1)$ and $(2,1)$; Proposition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form} with the fixed loci of Remark \claimref{note.transport.where-each-stratum-comes}, and Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}; and the two consistency checks of the section ``Consistency checks against known theory''.

The eight checks of the section ``One-dimensional extensions: where the obstruction lies, and the commuting square'' cover: Theorem \claimref{transport.where-obstruction-lies-commuting-square}(a) on every even-dimensional $(p,q)$ with $2 \leq n \leq 6$, with Corollary \claimref{transport.which-residues-obstruct-which-way}'s two residue sets read off the grid, Corollary \claimref{transport.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-one-real} in dimensions $3, 5, 7, 9, 11$, and Remark \claimref{note.transport.three-dimensions}'s three cases; Lemma \claimref{transport.even-subalgebra-one-dimensional-extension} on $(1,3)$ and $(2,0)$ with both signs of $\nu^2$; and Theorem \claimref{transport.where-obstruction-lies-commuting-square}(c), (d) on the whole grid, the repairs built from the signature tuple of the extension found to obstruct, with Proposition \claimref{transport.fusion-occurs-most-once} along the square (the centre of $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ computed blade-wise and found trivial, so fusion occurs at most once).

The script checks named identities in named signatures, exactly and exhaustively within the range it enumerates; the Lean file proves the quantified statements, for every associative ring, every element, every transport history, and every $(p,q)$. t02-regenerated.text: Projective geometric algebra $\Cl(3,0,1)$ and conformal geometric algebra $\Cl(4,1)$ are the two standard algebras of applied geometric computing, usually presented as independent modelling choices. This note proves that the second is the unique minimal nondegenerate completion of the first. For any real Clifford algebra $\Cl(p,q,r)$ of a degenerate form with nondegenerate part of signature $(p,q)$ and radical of dimension $r$, the minimal nondegenerate Clifford completion exists, has signature exactly $(p{+}r, q{+}r)$, and is unique up to an isometry fixing the original space pointwise: existence by adjoining the dual of the radical with the hyperbolic pairing, minimality because each radical direction must pair nontrivially into any completion, the signature forced by Witt splitting of the complement, and uniqueness by the Witt extension theorem. In particular $\Cl(3,0,1)$ completes minimally and uniquely to $\Cl(4,1)$. The completion converts the radical's nilpotent ideal into the unit ideal. No extension gives a radical element an inverse, since its square stays zero; what CGA supplies is a partner $\varphi$ for each radical direction $\rho$ with $\rho\varphi + \varphi\rho = 2$, so the division PGA lacks becomes total at the level of ideals, through the pairing and not through inverses. The embedding carries PGA's translators to CGA's translators verbatim. Every result is proved in full; the note situates the theorem in the series' transport-rule taxonomy and delimits what minimality promises. All computational identities are verified in exact rational arithmetic in an accompanying script.

t02-regenerated.title: Introduction
t02-regenerated.text:
Two algebras dominate applied geometric algebra. Projective (plane-based) geometric algebra, $\mathrm{PGA} = \Cl(3,0,1)$, models Euclidean rigid motions with a degenerate metric whose null direction $e_0$ encodes the plane at infinity \cite{Gunn2017, Selig2005}. Conformal geometric algebra, $\mathrm{CGA} = \Cl(4,1)$, embeds Euclidean space on a null quadric and adds inversions and dilations to the versor group \cite{HLR2001, DFM2007}. The two are normally introduced as alternative modelling decisions with different trade-offs. This note proves a sharper statement: CGA is the \emph{unique minimal nondegenerate completion} of PGA. The relationship is a theorem, an instance of the general minimal-completion theorem for degenerate Clifford algebras, which this note states and proves in full (Theorem \claimref{conformal.minimal-nondegenerate-completion}), with the PGA case as its principal corollary (Corollary \claimref{conformal.principal-case}).

The theorem belongs to a series. The root paper \cite{ButlerT1} proved the transport principle, that the failure of division at null vectors of $\Cl(p,q)$ is repaired minimally and uniquely by one hyperbolic plane, $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, and classified all zero-divisor obstructions and their transport rules; the sheaf paper \cite{ButlerT4} handled metrics that degenerate along a locus, where the radical generates a canonical square-zero ideal (the corank-one case), and proved that any nondegenerate completion converts that ideal into the unit ideal. The present note is the degenerate-algebra instance of the same programme: a radical of dimension $r$ requires exactly $r$ hyperbolic planes, and the minimal completion is unique. What is new here is the full rigor: the minimality argument is completed, the signature is forced by a Witt-splitting argument, and uniqueness is proved by the Witt extension theorem, none of which the applied literature states in this generality.

t02-regenerated.title: Minimal nondegenerate completion
t02-regenerated.proof:
\emph{(1) The radical pairing.} Let $(\widetilde W, Q)$ be any completion. For $\rho \in R$ the functional $Q(\rho, \cdot)$ vanishes on all of $W$ (it equals $B(\rho, \cdot)$ there), hence descends to a functional on $\widetilde W / W$. This defines a linear map
\[
\lambda : R \longrightarrow (\widetilde W / W)^*, \qquad \lambda(\rho) := Q(\rho, \cdot) \bmod W .
\]
If $\lambda(\rho) = 0$ then $Q(\rho, \cdot)$ vanishes on $W$ and on representatives of $\widetilde W / W$, hence on $\widetilde W$, so $\rho = 0$ by nondegeneracy: $\lambda$ is injective, and $\dim(\widetilde W / W) \geq r$.

\emph{(2) Existence at the bound, and the forced signature.} Take $\widetilde W := W \oplus R^*$ and define $Q$ by: $Q|_W = B$; $Q(\rho, \varphi) = \varphi(\rho)$ for $\rho \in R$, $\varphi \in R^*$; $Q(\varphi, \varphi') = 0$ on $R^*$; and $Q(V_1, R^*) = 0$ for a fixed complement $V_1$ of $R$ in $W$. Nondegeneracy: if $v_1 + \rho + \varphi$ ($v_1 \in V_1$, $\rho \in R$, $\varphi \in R^*$) is $Q$-orthogonal to everything, then pairing against $R^*$ gives $\rho = 0$, against $R$ gives $\varphi = 0$, and against $V_1$ gives $v_1 = 0$ since $B|_{V_1}$ is nondegenerate (it is a complement of the radical). For the signature, choose a basis $\rho_1, \dots, \rho_r$ of $R$ with dual basis $\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_r$: each $\operatorname{span}\{\rho_i, \varphi_i\}$ is a hyperbolic plane, the planes are mutually orthogonal and orthogonal to $V_1$, so $Q \cong B|_{V_1} \perp H^{\perp r}$ has signature $(p{+}r, q{+}r)$.

Now let $(\widetilde W, Q)$ be \emph{any} completion of dimension $m + r$. Then $V_1^{\perp}$ (orthocomplement in $\widetilde W$) is nondegenerate of dimension $(m{+}r) - (p{+}q) = 2r$, being the orthocomplement of a nondegenerate subspace, and it contains $R$ (radical vectors are $B$-orthogonal to $V_1$), which is totally isotropic of dimension $r$: half the dimension. We claim:
\begin{quote}
\emph{a nondegenerate quadratic space $(X, Q_X)$ of dimension $2s$ containing a totally isotropic subspace $U$ of dimension $s$ is isometric to $H^{\perp s}$.}
\end{quote}
The claim with $s = r$ gives $Q|_{V_1^\perp} \cong H^{\perp r}$ of signature $(r,r)$, and the total is $(p{+}r, q{+}r)$.

Proof of the claim, by induction on $s$, the case $s = 0$ being empty. \begin{cases}

\pm\, (x_T\, x_{T'})\; \rho_{S \cup S'} & \text{if } S \cap S' = \emptyset ,
\end{cases}

t03-regenerated.title: Introduction
t03-regenerated.text:
The root paper of the series \cite{ButlerT1} repairs the failure of division at the null cone of $\Cl(p,q)$ by the minimal Witt completion $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, shows this is one of exactly two transport rules, classifies what each adjoins, and proves that the completed algebra is the matrix amplification $\Mat_2(\Cl(p,q))$ with the base embedded as a twisted diagonal. The completed algebra, being a Clifford algebra of mixed signature, has a null cone of its own. The question this paper answers is the evident one: what happens when the transport is iterated? Three specific forms of the question: does the ascended algebra's own singular behaviour force a further ascent, without end; does the mod-8 periodicity of the real Clifford classification make the climb circulate; and what is the limit object?

The answers are more specific than the questions. The tower $\Cl(p{+}k,q{+}k)$ is canonically $\Mat_{2^k}(\Cl(p,q))$, so the climb never leaves the ground floor's Morita class: the clock is frozen, not circulating, and the eight clock positions classify eight parallel towers, one per transport charge $p - q \bmod 8$, rather than eight stages of one tower. What the iteration accumulates is capacity, not algebraic type: each rung adjoins one hyperbolic plane whose ladder pair satisfies the canonical anticommutation relations exactly, the Fock module doubles, and the Witt index, the algebra's count of independent fermionic modes, increases by exactly one. The limit is then the object the physical reading requires: the ground algebra tensored with the CAR algebra of a free fermionic field. Iterated transport is second quantisation, one mode per rung.

The mathematical content of the limit statement requires operator-algebraic care, which it receives here. The connecting embeddings are twisted diagonals $a \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(a, \hat a)$, with $\hat a$ the grade involution; whether the twist can be removed decides whether the limit is a plain tensor product. For even transport charge the ground algebra is central simple, the involution is inner by the Skolem-Noether theorem, and the twist conjugates away rung by rung: the algebraic limit is exactly $\Cl(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^\infty}$, and its completed complexification is $\Cl(p,q)_\C \otimes \CAR$. For odd charge the grade involution acts nontrivially on the centre and is outer; the even-charge argument does not apply, and rather than assert the unproved standard expectation we delimit the boundary and pose the odd case precisely.

t03-regenerated.title: Volume elements of the planes
t03-regenerated.text: Let $\omega_j = e_j f_j$. Then $\omega_j^2 = 1$; $\omega_j$ anticommutes with $e_j$ and $f_j$; $\omega_j$ commutes with $e_i, f_i$ for $i \neq j$ and with every ground generator; and the $\omega_j$ commute pairwise.
